title: Segment Tree Query and Update Bounds
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: With n leaves, a segment tree answers range queries and performs point updates in O(log n) time and uses O(n) space.
short: Tree height is logarithmic and queries touch few nodes.
long: Tree height is logarithmic and queries touch few nodes. An implicit heap layout uses at most 4n nodes.
proof: A range query visits at most two root-to-leaf paths plus their side branches; a point update follows one path.
consequence: The bounds make segment trees a workhorse of competitive and systems programming.

title: Lazy Propagation for Range Updates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Storing pending updates at covered segment-tree nodes and pushing them down only when needed supports range add and range sum in O(log n) per operation.
short: Defer work until a child is actually visited.
long: Defer work until a child is actually visited. Without laziness, a range update would touch O(k log n) elements explicitly.
proof: A range update marks O(log n) canonical nodes; the stored tags are applied during later traversals.
consequence: Lazy propagation extends segment trees to range-assignment and range-add workloads.

title: Linear-Time Segment Tree Construction
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Filling leaves and computing internal nodes bottom-up builds a segment tree in O(n) time.
short: One pass over internal nodes suffices.
long: One pass over internal nodes suffices. Repeated point updates would build the same tree in O(n log n).
proof: There are n-1 internal nodes, each computed in constant time from its two children.
consequence: Construction is never the bottleneck in segment-tree applications.

title: Persistent Segment Tree Versions
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Copying only the O(log n) nodes on a modified root-to-leaf path creates a new version of a segment tree in O(log n) time and space.
short: Path copying shares all untouched subtrees.
long: Path copying shares all untouched subtrees. Old versions remain queryable, enabling time-travel queries such as range k-th statistics over prefixes.
proof: Nodes outside the updated path are immutable and can be shared safely between versions.
consequence: Persistence adds historical queries at logarithmic overhead.

title: Sparse Dynamic Segment Tree
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: When only a few positions of a huge coordinate range are set, allocating nodes lazily along update paths uses O(k log U) space for k updates in a universe U.
short: Do not materialise empty intervals.
long: Do not materialise empty intervals. It supports the same O(log U) operations as a full segment tree on sparse data.
proof: Each update creates at most one node per level of the coordinate tree.
consequence: Dynamic segment trees handle 64-bit coordinate spaces without allocating terabytes.

title: Two-Dimensional Fenwick Tree
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Nesting Fenwick trees over rows and columns supports point updates and rectangle-sum queries on an n by m grid in O(log n log m) time.
short: Apply the one-dimensional trick in both coordinates.
long: Apply the one-dimensional trick in both coordinates. Space is O(nm), and sparse maps can reduce it for large sparse grids.
proof: A rectangle sum is a combination of four 2D prefix sums, each computed with nested lowbit loops.
consequence: 2D BITs are standard for offline counting and dynamic frequency grids.

title: Range Tree for Orthogonal Queries
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A 2D range tree is a balanced tree on x-coordinates with each node storing a secondary sorted structure on the y-coordinates of its subtree.
short: A tree of sorted lists answers rectangle queries.
long: A tree of sorted lists answers rectangle queries. All points of a node's subtree are sorted by y for reporting points in an x-range and y-range.
proof: An x-range decomposes into O(log n) canonical nodes, each searched in its y-list.
consequence: Range trees solve orthogonal range reporting and counting in logarithmic-ish time.

title: Range Tree Query Complexity
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A 2D range tree reports k points in an orthogonal rectangle in O(log^2 n + k) time using O(n log n) space.
short: Logarithmic search at each of logarithmically many nodes.
long: Logarithmic search at each of logarithmically many nodes. In d dimensions the bound generalises to O(log^d n + k) with O(n log^{d-1} n) space.
proof: There are O(log n) canonical x-nodes and each secondary search costs O(log n) plus output.
consequence: It is the baseline for comparing specialised spatial indexes.

title: Fractional Cascading in Range Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Adding pointers between corresponding entries of sorted child lists reduces 2D range reporting to O(log n + k) time.
short: Reuse the search position from one list in the next.
long: Reuse the search position from one list in the next. The extra pointers increase space by a constant factor only.
proof: A binary search at the root yields candidate ranks that can be followed downward via cascade pointers in O(1) per level.
consequence: Fractional cascading removes one logarithmic factor from many multi-level searches.

title: Wavelet Tree Sequence Statistics
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A wavelet tree recursively partitions an alphabet, storing at each node a bitvector recording which branch each sequence element takes.
short: Binary search over the alphabet, with bitvectors per level.
long: Binary search over the alphabet, with bitvectors per level. It supports rank, select, access, quantile and range counting in O(log sigma) time.
proof: Each level halves the alphabet, so the tree has depth log sigma and bitvector ranks navigate it.
consequence: Wavelet trees provide compressed, fast indexes for strings and sequences.

title: Merge Sort Tree for Range Counting
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Storing the sorted list of each segment-tree node lets a range count values below x in O(log^2 n) time using O(n log n) space.
short: Segment tree nodes act as pre-sorted summaries.
long: Segment tree nodes act as pre-sorted summaries. Range k-th smallest can be found by binary searching the answer value with these counts.
proof: The query interval decomposes into O(log n) nodes and each binary search costs O(log n).
consequence: It is a simple static solution to range quantile and counting queries.

title: Mo's Algorithm for Offline Range Queries
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Sorting queries by block of left endpoint and then by right endpoint lets all q range queries on a static array be answered with O((n+q) sqrt n) pointer moves.
short: Reuse a sliding interval between similar queries.
long: Reuse a sliding interval between similar queries. It applies when queries can be reordered and the aggregate supports cheap add/remove of one element.
proof: Right endpoints move at most n times per left-block, and there are O(n/sqrt n) blocks, giving O(n sqrt n) moves.
consequence: It is a standard offline trick for range-distinct and range-mode problems.

title: Sqrt Decomposition Array Updates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Splitting an array into blocks of size about sqrt n supports range add by adjusting whole-block tags and point queries in O(sqrt n) time.
short: Coarse block summaries plus small boundary scans.
long: Coarse block summaries plus small boundary scans. It is easy to implement and often fast due to good constants.
proof: A range covers at most O(sqrt n) whole blocks and at most 2sqrt n boundary elements.
consequence: It provides a simple fallback where segment trees are overkill.

title: Link-Cut Tree Dynamic Forest Operations
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Link-cut trees represent dynamic forests and support link, cut, path aggregate and connectivity queries in O(log n) amortised time.
short: Represented paths as splay trees enable dynamic tree queries.
long: Represented paths as splay trees enable dynamic tree queries. They do not support general graph updates, only forests.
proof: Preferred paths are stored in splay trees, and splay operations rebalance after each access.
consequence: They enable dynamic network flows and online tree path queries.

title: Euler Tour Tree for Dynamic Connectivity
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Representing each tree by its Euler tour in a balanced BST supports link, cut and connectivity queries in O(log n) amortised time.
short: A tree becomes a sequence of directed edges.
long: A tree becomes a sequence of directed edges. Link and cut splice Euler-tour sequences; component membership is read from the represented tree.
proof: Rotations in the sequence correspond to rerooting, and balanced BST splits and merges take logarithmic time.
consequence: ET-trees are an alternative to link-cut trees for dynamic forests.

title: Heavy-Light Decomposition of Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Choosing the largest child as heavy decomposes any root-to-leaf path into O(log n) light-edge segments that map to contiguous array ranges.
short: Convert tree paths into a few array intervals.
long: Convert tree paths into a few array intervals. Each light edge at least halves subtree size, bounding their number on a path.
proof: Following a light edge moves into a subtree of at most half the size, so at most log n such edges occur.
consequence: It reduces path queries on a static tree to segment-tree range queries.

title: Link-Cut versus Heavy-Light Trade-off
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Heavy-light decomposition is simpler and gives deterministic O(log^2 n) path queries on static trees, while link-cut trees allow topology changes at amortised O(log n) cost.
short: Static simplicity versus dynamic flexibility.
long: Static simplicity versus dynamic flexibility. Link-cut trees have larger constants and more subtle invariants.
proof: Heavy-light relies on fixed subtree sizes; link-cut trees rebalance preferred paths dynamically.
consequence: Choose based on whether the underlying tree ever changes.

title: Disjoint Sparse Table for Static RMQ
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A disjoint sparse table answers idempotent static range queries in O(1) time with O(n log n) preprocessing and space.
short: Precompute suffixes and prefixes inside disjoint blocks.
long: Precompute suffixes and prefixes inside disjoint blocks. Unlike a standard sparse table, it handles overlapping queries of any length with two precomputed blocks.
proof: A range crossing a power-of-two boundary is covered by two precomputed half-block aggregates.
consequence: It is an alternative constant-time RMQ structure with simple preprocessing.

title: Sparse Tables Are Static Only
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Changing one array element invalidates Theta(n log n) sparse-table entries, so the structure cannot support efficient updates.
short: Constant-time queries come at the price of immutability.
long: Constant-time queries come at the price of immutability. Dynamic RMQ needs segment trees or Fischer–Heun style structures with different trade-offs.
proof: Each level of the sparse table stores overlapping blocks that all contain the updated index.
consequence: Check update requirements before choosing a static RMQ structure.

title: Persistent Balanced Search Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Path copying in an AVL or red-black tree produces a fully persistent ordered map with O(log n) time and space per update.
short: Immutable nodes let every version coexist.
long: Immutable nodes let every version coexist. Balance fields are recomputed on the copied path; rotation may create a constant number of extra nodes.
proof: Only nodes on the modified root-to-leaf path change, so sharing the rest preserves all invariants.
consequence: Persistent maps underpin functional collections and versioned databases.

title: Rollback Union-Find
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Recording parent and rank changes lets union-find undo the most recent unions, enabling divide-and-conquer and rollback-based offline algorithms.
short: Log changes and rewind when leaving a recursion branch.
long: Log changes and rewind when leaving a recursion branch. Path compression is usually disabled or carefully logged because it complicates rollback.
proof: Each union changes a constant number of fields, so a stack of changes suffices to restore prior state.
consequence: It is used in offline dynamic connectivity and segment-tree-over-time solutions.

title: Online Dynamic Connectivity with ET-Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Euler tour trees maintain connectivity under link and cut operations in an amortised O(log^2 n) per update in the worst case.
short: Balanced Euler tours support online topology changes.
long: Balanced Euler tours support online topology changes. Faster randomised and deterministic structures exist, but ET-trees are conceptually simple.
proof: Link and cut are split-and-merge operations on balanced BST sequences, with logarithmic overhead per structural change.
consequence: They handle connectivity when updates arrive without knowledge of the future.

title: LSM Tree Write Amplification
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: LSM trees absorb writes in an in-memory memtable and flush sorted runs, so a logical write may be physically written several times during compaction.
short: Cheap writes are paid for later by merging runs.
long: Cheap writes are paid for later by merging runs. Write amplification is the ratio of bytes written to storage to bytes written by the application.
proof: Each level merge rewrites existing data along with new data, multiplying physical writes.
consequence: Compaction policy trades write amplification against read and space amplification.

title: LSM Tree Read Path
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: An LSM lookup checks the memtable and then successive on-disk levels, often using bloom filters to skip levels that cannot contain the key.
short: Newest data is checked first; filters prune older runs.
long: Newest data is checked first; filters prune older runs. Point lookups can touch many levels, while range scans merge iterators across runs.
proof: Each level is a sorted immutable run, so a binary search per level locates candidate entries.
consequence: Bloom filters are essential to keep point-read latency acceptable.

title: LSM Compaction Strategies
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Size-tiered compaction merges similarly sized runs to favour writes, while leveled compaction maintains one sorted level per size to favour reads.
short: Choose which amplification to minimise.
long: Choose which amplification to minimise. Leveled designs reduce read and space amplification at the cost of more write amplification.
proof: Merging runs of equal size rewrites each byte once per level in leveled designs, bounding overlap.
consequence: The choice dominates the behaviour of modern key-value stores.
